original_value: This research tested how different scanner positions and sample plot sizes affect the tree detection and diameter measurement in forest inventories. For this, a multistage density-based clustering approach was further developed for the automatic mapping of tree positions and simultaneously applied with automatic measurements of tree diameters. This further development of the algorithm reduced the proportion of falsely detected tree locations by about 64%. The algorithms were tested in different settings with respect to the number and spatial alignment of scanner positions and under manifold forest conditions, covering different age classes and a mixture of scenarios, and representing a broad gradient of structural complexity. For circular sample plots with a maximum radius of 20 m, the tree mapping algorithm showed a detection rate of 82.4% with seven scanner positions at the vertices of a hexagon plus the center coordinates, and 68.3% with four scanner positions aligned in a triangle plus the center. Detection rates were significantly increased with smaller maximum radii. Thus, with a maximum radius of 10 m, the hexagon setting yielded a detection rate of 90.5% and the triangle 92%. Other alignments of scanner positions were also tested, but proved to be either unfavorable or too labor-intensive. The commission rates were on average less than 3%. The root mean square error (RMSE) of the dbh (diameter at breast height) measurement was between 2.66 cm and 4.18 cm for the hexagon and between 3.0 cm and 4.7 cm for the triangle design. The robustness of the algorithm was also demonstrated via tests by means of an international benchmark dataset. It has been shown that the number of stems per hectare had a significant impact on the detection rate.

result.paraphrase: The study examined how scanner placement and sample plot size influence tree detection and diameter measurement in forest inventories. To do so, a multistage density-based clustering method was further refined for automated tree-position mapping and used alongside automatic tree-diameter measurements. This algorithmic enhancement lowered the share of false tree detections by roughly 64%. The methods were evaluated under varying numbers and spatial arrangements of scanner positions and across diverse forest conditions, including different age classes and mixed scenarios, representing a wide gradient of structural complexity. For circular sample plots with a maximum radius of 20 m, the mapping algorithm achieved a detection rate of 82.4% with seven scanner positions arranged at the vertices of a hexagon plus the center, and 68.3% with four scanner positions arranged in a triangle plus the center. Detection rates increased significantly when the maximum radius was reduced. At a 10 m maximum radius, the hexagon setup reached 90.5% and the triangle setup 92%. Other scanner arrangements were also tested, but proved either disadvantageous or too labor-intensive. On average, commission rates were below 3%. The RMSE for dbh (diameter at breast height) measurements ranged from 2.66 cm to 4.18 cm in the hexagon design and from 3.0 cm to 4.7 cm in the triangle design. The algorithm’s robustness was further confirmed using an international benchmark dataset. It was also demonstrated that stems per hectare had a significant effect on detection rate.
